title: Training cross-validated skill predicted forward skill of climate relations in runoff, phenology and dengue but not butterflies, and did not beat a response-class rule (4,399 pre-registered tests)
abstract: Question: can an honest training-period skill estimate tell which climate-response relations keep forecast skill in later years, and does it do better than response class? Approach: we froze and timestamped a plan before any outcome. We applied one procedure to 4,399 annual series from four systems, one response class each: Australian catchment runoff (abiotic, 266), Swiss plant phenology (timing, 1,780), UK butterfly site abundance (population, 2,283) and national dengue cases (disease, 70). For each series we selected one of 120 monthly temperature or precipitation windows in early years and scored the frozen model in later years (for example 1996-2024) against the training mean. The screen was nested rolling-origin skill in training years, with the window selection repeated at each origin. Results: the in-sample R2 of the selected window was optimistic by 0.14-0.78 skill units. The nested screen was nearly unbiased. The screen ranked forward skill within runoff (Spearman 0.30), phenology (0.32) and dengue (0.48), but not within butterflies (0.01; test slopes kept their sign in 58% of series). Across systems the screen did not beat the class rule (sign accuracy 0.721 vs 0.684, difference CI -0.000 to 0.074), and family explained more forward-skill variance than the screen (0.21 vs 0.09). In all four systems a trailing 10-year mean beat the training mean (median gain 0.13-0.67). Frozen climate terms captured at least half of the level shift mainly in phenology (58% of series). A later split gave the same decisions. Conclusion: a positive nested screen is necessary but not sufficient. Relations must also be stable in time, and level updates are needed. Limitations: one system per class, shared years make intervals too narrow, observed rather than forecast weather, simple one-window models.

display.caption: Training nested-CV skill (P1_cv) against forward skill (F1, frozen model vs training mean) for 4,399 series in four systems. Black dots: quintile medians. Open squares: the same quintiles at in-sample R2. The screen ranks forward skill in runoff, phenology and dengue, but not in butterflies.

Medians of in-sample R2, nested-CV skill, forward skill and the level gain of a trailing mean, with 95% cluster-bootstrap intervals. Crosses: permuted-response null. In-sample R2 is optimistic; the nested screen is close to later forward skill; level gains are positive in all four systems.

Left: accuracy of the training screen (P1_cv > 0) and of the response-class rule for the sign of forward skill. Right: share of series with forward gain among screen-positive (filled) and screen-negative (open) series.

citations.reason: Previous test of the response-class rule. We test its post hoc signal-fraction and level-shift explanations prospectively at scale; the screen did not beat the class rule.
